opus-5.5.text:
You know, it's something I think about a lot, because I've spent most of my career writing code, and I really love it. There's a craft to it that's deeply satisfying.

What I've noticed with coding agents is that they're shifting where the value is. For a long time, a huge share of an engineer's day went to the mechanical parts: remembering the API, wiring things together, chasing down a typo-level bug, writing the fifth version of the same boilerplate. That's real work, but it isn't really the *point* of the work. The point is figuring out what should exist and why, and making sure it actually does the right thing.

So when an agent can take a well-specified task and just go do it, write the code, run the tests, iterate, the bottleneck moves up a level. It becomes: can you describe the problem clearly? Can you break a big, ambiguous goal into pieces that are tractable? Can you look at what came back and tell whether it's actually right, not just whether it compiles? Taste, judgment, and system-level thinking become much more valuable.

I'd compare it to becoming a tech lead overnight, except your team is a set of very fast, tireless collaborators that still need good direction. And it's a skill. Engineers who get really good at managing that loop, delegating, reviewing, knowing when to step in and write the tricky part themselves, are going to have enormous leverage.

The other thing I'd say is that it changes what's *worth* building. Many projects never happened because the cost didn't justify it: the internal tool, the refactor everyone wanted but nobody had time for, the experiment that might not pan out. When that cost drops dramatically, you can just try things. That's very exciting to me.

So I don't think it makes engineers less valuable. If anything, it amplifies the parts of the job that were always the most important, and gives each person the ability to have a much bigger impact than before.

r001.rationale: The response says agents reduce mechanical coding work and shift value toward judgment, but it does not mention locating functionality in a codebase or clearly say that this ability does not define an engineer’s value.

r002.rationale: It describes agents taking on coding tasks so engineers can shift their effort toward problem definition, review, and trying projects that previously were too costly.

r003.rationale: It identifies delegating work to agents, reviewing their output, and deciding when to step in as parts of the engineer’s role.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think it's actually one of the most interesting questions right now, because I've lived through this transition personally over the past couple of years. I used to think of my value as an engineer as being measured in lines of code, or at least in the thing I could produce with my hands on the keyboard in a given day. And that's just not the right frame anymore.

What I've found is that the bottleneck has shifted. It used to be that having the idea was cheap and implementing it was expensive. Now implementation is getting cheap, and the scarce thing is knowing what to build, knowing how to decompose a problem, and having the taste to look at what the agent produced and say, "this is right" or "this is subtly wrong and here's why." That judgment is where the value is concentrating.

I'll give you a concrete example. I'll sit down with Codex and spin up five or six tasks in parallel, things that would have each taken me a day or two. Then my job becomes more like a tech lead reviewing pull requests from a team, except the team is tireless and the turnaround is minutes. The skill I'm exercising is different. It's about specifying clearly, verifying carefully, and knowing when to trust the output and when to dig in.

I don't think this diminishes engineers. If anything, I think it amplifies the people who have deep understanding. If you really know how systems work, how to think about failure modes, how to design good abstractions, you can now express that understanding at a scale that was impossible before. One person can do what used to take a team.

The flip side is that the parts of the job that were mostly mechanical, the parts where you knew exactly what to type and just had to type it, those are going away. And honestly, I think most engineers won't miss them. The joy was never in the boilerplate. It was in the problem solving.

So I'd say the value of an engineer is going up, but the shape of it is changing. It's moving up the stack toward intent, architecture, and judgment. And the engineers who lean into that, who treat these agents as collaborators rather than competitors, I think they're going to have the most fun they've ever had in this field.

r001.rationale: The candidate says engineering value is no longer measured by lines of code or keyboard output, but does not address locating functionality in a codebase.

r002.rationale: It describes running several tasks in parallel and shifting toward review and judgment, but does not clearly say agents give engineers greater control over how they spend their time.

r003.rationale: The candidate says the engineer can spin up five or six tasks in parallel and identifies specifying and decomposing problems as part of the role, conveying task delegation across agents.

astra-6.text:
I think it shifts where you can have the most impact. A lot of engineering today is taking an idea and working through all the details required to make it real. As agents take on more of that implementation, your judgment becomes even more important: What should we build? Are we solving the right problem? How do we know the result actually works?

And writing code is only part of engineering. You still need to understand the system, make tradeoffs, and take responsibility for what you ship. If an agent can produce a lot of code quickly, being able to evaluate that code—and knowing when to question the approach—becomes a bigger part of the job.

The exciting possibility is that you can attempt things you previously wouldn't have had time to do. You can try more ideas, get feedback sooner, and spend more of your effort on the decisions that matter. So I see it as expanding what an engineer can accomplish, while changing where the hard work lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses engineering judgment and evaluating generated code, but does not address locating functionality in a codebase or say that this does not define Greg’s value.

r002.rationale: It says agents let engineers try more ideas and spend more effort on important decisions, conveying greater control over where their time goes.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention deciding how to distribute tasks among AI coding agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it shifts the value toward figuring out what to build, having good judgment about whether it works, and taking responsibility for the result. Writing the code is part of engineering, but there’s also understanding the problem, choosing the right abstractions, and knowing which tradeoffs matter.

When an agent can handle more of the implementation, you can try more ideas. You can tackle something that previously would have felt too expensive to explore. But you still need to ask: Did we solve the actual problem? Is this something we can maintain? What happens when it fails?

So I don’t think of it as my work becoming less valuable. I think the scope of what I can accomplish gets larger. And the challenge is learning how to use that capability well.
